questions.why: Vocabulary: the tragedy is not certain to happen, as customary rules show.

paras: Children invent games long before anyone teaches them rules. A ball, a wall and a patch of open ground are enough; the rules are agreed, argued over and changed as the game goes on, and the point of playing is simply to go on playing. Organised sport takes this impulse and gives it structure: fixed rules, referees, leagues, coaches and, at the highest level, professional careers. The structure brings real benefits. It allows skill to be measured, rewards discipline and lets millions share the drama of a contest they could never play themselves.

Something can be lost in the process, however. When sport for the young is organised mainly as a pathway to selection, the child who is not chosen may conclude that sport is not for him at all, and give it up at the age when the habit of activity matters most. Practice becomes a duty to be completed rather than a pleasure to be sought, and the measure of success becomes the trophy rather than the game. None of this is an argument against coaching or competition. It is an argument for keeping, alongside the academy and the stadium, open spaces and unstructured hours in which anyone may play badly, cheerfully and for no reason beyond the enjoyment of it.

questions.q: The passage mainly argues that:
opts: Organised sport has real benefits, but space for free, unstructured play must also be kept.
Only professional sport deserves public support.
Coaching and competition harm young players.
Organised sport should be replaced by children's games.
questions.why: Main idea: the structure 'brings real benefits', yet the author argues 'for keeping... open spaces and unstructured hours'.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of organised sport?
opts: It lets millions share the drama of a contest.
It guarantees a professional career to every participant.
It allows skill to be measured.
It rewards discipline.
questions.why: Detail: the three benefits listed are measuring skill, rewarding discipline and sharing drama; careers come only 'at the highest level'.

questions.q: According to the passage, a child who is not selected may:
opts: Win more trophies in other sports.
Demand that the rules be changed.
Give up physical activity at an age when the habit matters most.
Become a better coach in later life.
questions.why: Inference/detail: the child 'may conclude that sport is not for him at all, and give it up at the age when the habit of activity matters most'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards coaching and competition is best described as:
opts: Opposing them as harmful to children.
Praising them as the only purpose of sport.
Indifferent to their effects on the young.
Accepting them, while warning against making selection their chief aim.
questions.why: Tone: 'None of this is an argument against coaching or competition', but against sport 'organised mainly as a pathway to selection'.

questions.q: The word "impulse" in the passage most nearly means:
opts: Sudden injury
Cash reward
Natural urge
Written rule
questions.why: Vocabulary: organised sport takes the children's spontaneous urge to play and gives it structure.

paras: Fitness has come to be associated with special places and special clothing: the gymnasium with its machines, the running track, the class that meets at six in the morning. These have their uses, but they can obscure a simpler truth. For most of human history people were active not because they exercised but because their lives required it. They walked to fields and markets, carried water, ground grain and climbed hills. Physical activity was woven into the day rather than added to it as a separate task.

Many people today spend their waking hours seated, at a desk, in a vehicle or before a screen, and then try to compensate with an hour of vigorous effort. The hour is worth having, but it may not undo the effects of the remaining sedentary day. A growing body of opinion holds that the small movements of daily life matter more than was once assumed: climbing stairs instead of taking the lift, walking to the shop, standing up every half hour, doing household chores by hand. Such activity is unglamorous and earns no medals, but it has the advantage of being sustainable, since it demands no fees, no equipment and no special motivation. The aim, perhaps, is not to become an athlete but to recover a little of the ordinary movement that modern convenience has quietly taken away.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: Choosing the Right Gymnasium
Why Exercise Is a Waste of Time
A History of Athletics
Movement Woven into the Day
questions.why: Main idea: ordinary daily movement, once 'woven into the day', deserves to be recovered.

questions.q: According to the passage, for most of human history people were active because:
opts: They wished to win medals.
They attended exercise classes.
They were advised to by physicians.
Their lives required it.
questions.why: Detail: 'people were active not because they exercised but because their lives required it'.

questions.q: The author suggests that an hour of vigorous exercise after a seated day:
opts: Fully cancels the effects of sitting.
Is useless and should be avoided.
Is more sustainable than daily movement.
Is worth having but may not be enough by itself.
questions.why: Inference: 'The hour is worth having, but it may not undo the effects of the remaining sedentary day'.

questions.q: The phrase "modern convenience has quietly taken away" suggests that:
opts: Convenience has made people more active.
Modern conveniences have been banned.
The loss of everyday movement happened gradually and largely unnoticed.
People deliberately chose to stop moving.
questions.why: Inference/tone: 'quietly' implies the change crept in without people noticing.

questions.q: The word "sedentary" most nearly means:
opts: Spent mostly sitting
Tiring
Healthy
Irregular
questions.why: Vocabulary: people 'spend their waking hours seated, at a desk, in a vehicle or before a screen'.

paras: A newspaper that never prints a correction is not a newspaper that never makes mistakes. Reporting is done in haste, from sources who may be confused, partial or simply wrong, and even careful journalists misread figures, misspell names and misattribute quotations. The question is not whether errors occur but how they are handled once discovered. A publication that corrects its mistakes openly, in a place where readers will see them, signals that it values accuracy above its own reputation for infallibility. Paradoxically, this frankness tends to increase rather than diminish public trust.

The digital age has made the problem both easier and harder. An online article can be amended within minutes, but it can also be amended silently, so that readers who saw the first version never learn that it was wrong. Meanwhile the original error may already have been copied, shared and quoted far beyond the publisher's reach. Responsible outlets now note at the foot of an article what was changed and when, and some maintain public records of their corrections. Such practices may seem a small matter of housekeeping. They are, in fact, part of the bargain between the press and its readers: the press asks to be believed, and in return it must show that it takes the trouble to be right, and to say so when it was not.

questions.q: The central idea of the passage is that:
opts: Openly correcting errors is essential to the credibility of the press.
Online journalism is less accurate than print.
Journalists should never rely on sources.
Newspapers that print corrections are careless.
questions.why: Main idea: open correction 'tends to increase rather than diminish public trust' and is 'part of the bargain between the press and its readers'.

questions.q: According to the passage, a problem particular to online articles is that they can be:
opts: Read only by a small audience.
Corrected only after several weeks.
Printed only once a day.
Amended silently, so earlier readers never learn of the error.
questions.why: Detail: 'it can also be amended silently, so that readers who saw the first version never learn that it was wrong'.

questions.q: The author would most likely regard an outlet that quietly edits errors without any notice as:
opts: Following the best modern practice.
Failing in its obligation to its readers.
Protecting its readers from confusion.
Doing a harmless piece of housekeeping.
questions.why: Inference: responsible outlets 'note... what was changed and when'; the press must 'say so when it was not' right.

questions.q: The author calls the effect of open corrections "paradoxical" because:
opts: Corrections make newspapers more expensive.
One would expect admitting mistakes to reduce trust, yet it increases it.
Readers rarely notice corrections.
Corrections are usually wrong themselves.
questions.why: Inference: 'Paradoxically, this frankness tends to increase rather than diminish public trust'.

questions.q: The word "infallibility" most nearly means:
opts: Impartiality
Inability to be wrong
Speed of reporting
Popularity
questions.why: Vocabulary: the reputation of never making mistakes, which open correction gives up.

paras: Not long ago, millets such as ragi, jowar and bajra were dismissed in many Indian cities as the food of the poor, to be replaced by polished rice and refined wheat as soon as a family could afford them. The change was understandable. White rice and soft wheat bread were quicker to cook, easier to digest for those unused to coarse grains, and carried the prestige of prosperity. Government procurement and distribution, which favoured rice and wheat for decades, reinforced the shift, and in many regions farmers turned land once sown with millets to more profitable crops.

Opinion has since begun to turn. Millets are now praised for their fibre and minerals, and for the modest demands they make on the farmer: many grow on poor soils with little water and tolerate heat that would wither other cereals. Recipes once kept by grandmothers are reappearing in restaurants and packaged foods. The revival is welcome, but it carries a certain irony. A grain that was abandoned because it signalled poverty is being rediscovered partly because it now signals discernment, and the price of some millet products in city shops would surprise the farmers who grow them. If the revival is to last, it will need to reach ordinary kitchens and fields, and not remain a fashion for those who can afford to follow fashions.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: Cooking Techniques for Coarse Grains
The Return of the Humble Grain
Why Rice Is Healthier Than Millets
The Failure of Government Procurement
questions.why: Main idea: millets, once dismissed, are being revived.

questions.q: According to the passage, white rice and wheat replaced millets partly because they:
opts: Were cheaper than millets in every region.
Were quicker to cook and carried the prestige of prosperity.
Contained more fibre and minerals.
Grew on poorer soils with less water.
questions.why: Detail: they 'were quicker to cook, easier to digest... and carried the prestige of prosperity'.

questions.q: The "irony" mentioned in the passage is that:
opts: Grandmothers refuse to share their recipes.
Millets grow well only where water is plentiful.
Farmers now earn more from millets than anyone else.
A grain once rejected as a sign of poverty is now valued as a sign of refined taste.
questions.why: Inference: 'abandoned because it signalled poverty... rediscovered partly because it now signals discernment'.

questions.q: The author's chief concern about the millet revival is that it:
opts: May remain limited to affluent consumers instead of reaching ordinary households and farmers.
Is based on false claims about nutrition.
Will force farmers to stop growing millets.
Will make rice and wheat disappear entirely.
questions.why: Attitude: it must 'reach ordinary kitchens and fields, and not remain a fashion for those who can afford to follow fashions'.

questions.q: The word "discernment" most nearly means:
opts: Carelessness
Refined judgement
Hunger
Poverty
questions.why: Vocabulary: millets now signal good taste, the opposite of their earlier association with poverty.

paras: How can we tell a scientific theory from a merely confident opinion? One influential answer is that a scientific theory must take a risk. It must forbid certain things from happening, so that if those things are observed, the theory is shown to be false. The claim that all metals expand when heated is scientific in this sense: a single metal that contracted under heat would refute it. By contrast, a theory that can explain every possible outcome, whatever happens, has not thereby proved its strength. It has revealed that it says nothing definite about the world.

This criterion, usually called falsifiability, has a curious consequence. No number of confirming observations can establish a general theory beyond doubt, since the next observation might be the exception; yet one well-founded contrary observation can overturn it. Science, on this view, advances not by piling up proofs but by surviving attempts at refutation. Critics have pointed out that working scientists rarely abandon a theory at the first awkward result. They suspect their instruments, adjust auxiliary assumptions and wait for the anomaly to be explained, and sometimes they are right to do so. Even so, the central insight endures. A theory earns our trust not by being impossible to challenge but by having been exposed to challenge and having, so far, withstood it.

questions.q: The passage is mainly about:
opts: The idea that a scientific theory must be open to refutation and earns trust by surviving tests.
The impossibility of any scientific knowledge.
Why scientists distrust their instruments.
The physical properties of heated metals.
questions.why: Main idea: falsifiability; 'A theory earns our trust... by having been exposed to challenge and having, so far, withstood it'.

questions.q: Which example does the passage give of a scientific claim?
opts: Every possible outcome can be explained.
All metals expand when heated.
Confirming observations prove a theory.
Instruments are always reliable.
questions.why: Detail: 'The claim that all metals expand when heated is scientific in this sense'.

questions.q: The author would regard a theory that can explain every possible outcome as:
opts: Falsified by a single observation.
Proven beyond doubt.
The strongest kind of scientific theory.
Lacking definite content, rather than being especially strong.
questions.why: Inference: such a theory 'has not thereby proved its strength. It has revealed that it says nothing definite'.

questions.q: The critics mentioned in the passage point out that:
opts: In practice, scientists rarely discard a theory at the first contrary result.
Falsifiability makes every theory unscientific.
Scientific instruments never make errors.
Confirming observations can prove a theory beyond doubt.
questions.why: Detail: 'working scientists rarely abandon a theory at the first awkward result'.

questions.q: The word "auxiliary" in "adjust auxiliary assumptions" most nearly means:
opts: Purely mathematical
Supporting or secondary
False and misleading
Central and essential
questions.why: Vocabulary: scientists adjust the subsidiary assumptions around a theory rather than its core.

paras: A map that showed every pebble and blade of grass would be as large as the country it described, and therefore useless. Its value lies precisely in what it leaves out. Scientific models share this character. An economist's model of a market, a climatologist's model of the atmosphere, or a physicist's picture of a gas as countless tiny colliding balls all simplify the world deliberately, ignoring features judged irrelevant to the question at hand. The model of a gas as bouncing balls is false in many respects, yet it predicts how pressure changes with temperature remarkably well.

The danger arises when the simplification is forgotten. A model built to answer one question may be pressed into service for another for which its omissions are crucial, and its users, impressed by its past successes, may mistake the map for the territory. Many failures of forecasting, in economics especially, have been traced not to bad mathematics but to assumptions that were reasonable in ordinary times and disastrous in unusual ones. The remedy is not to abandon models, without which no complex system could be studied at all, but to use them with an awareness of their boundaries. A good scientist asks not only what a model predicts, but what it was designed to ignore.

opts: Models, Maps and Their Limits
Why Economists Cannot Do Mathematics
The Physics of Colliding Balls
How to Draw an Accurate Map
questions.why: Main idea: models, like maps, are useful because they simplify, but their limits must be remembered.

questions.q: The model of a gas as bouncing balls is mentioned as an example of a model that:
opts: Is accurate in every detail.
Is used mainly by economists.
Is false in many respects yet predicts well.
Has failed in every application.
questions.why: Detail: it 'is false in many respects, yet it predicts how pressure changes with temperature remarkably well'.

questions.q: To "mistake the map for the territory" means to:
opts: Draw a map larger than the country it shows.
Refuse to use any maps.
Lose one's way while travelling.
Treat a simplified representation as if it were reality itself.
questions.why: Inference: users 'impressed by its past successes' forget 'the simplification'.

questions.q: According to the passage, many failures of economic forecasting have been traced to:
opts: A shortage of computers.
Deliberate fraud by forecasters.
Bad mathematics.
Assumptions that suited ordinary times but failed in unusual ones.
questions.why: Detail: 'not to bad mathematics but to assumptions that were reasonable in ordinary times and disastrous in unusual ones'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards scientific models is best described as:
opts: Indifferent to how they are used.
Appreciative of their usefulness but alert to their limits.
Contemptuous, since all models are false.
Uncritically trusting of their predictions.
questions.why: Tone: 'The remedy is not to abandon models... but to use them with an awareness of their boundaries'.

paras: The traveller of earlier centuries set out with little more than a letter of introduction and a vague idea of the road. Delays were expected, routes changed with the weather, and much of what was seen had not been seen before by anyone the traveller knew. Today a journey can be planned to the hour. Reviews tell us where to eat, photographs show us in advance what each monument will look like, and a phone in the pocket ensures that we need never be lost. Few would wish to give up these conveniences, which have made travel safer and open to far more people than ever before.

Yet a journey fully known in advance risks becoming a kind of verification: we go to confirm that the place matches its picture. The encounters that travellers most often remember, by contrast, are the unplanned ones, such as the conversation with a stranger on a delayed train, the festival stumbled upon in a small town, or the meal in a house where no menu existed. These cannot be booked, only allowed for. The thoughtful traveller therefore leaves some of the day unscheduled and some of the map blank, not out of carelessness but as a deliberate act of openness. To travel well is not merely to arrive where one intended, but to be willing, now and then, to arrive somewhere one did not.

questions.q: The main idea of the passage is that:
opts: Earlier travellers were careless and ill-prepared.
Travel is safer today than ever before.
Modern planning has real value, but leaving room for the unplanned enriches travel.
Modern travel conveniences should be abandoned.
questions.why: Main idea: few would give up conveniences, yet 'the thoughtful traveller... leaves some of the day unscheduled'.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as an example of a memorable unplanned encounter?
opts: A guided tour of a famous monument.
A festival stumbled upon in a small town.
A hotel room booked months ahead.
A photograph taken at a famous viewpoint.
questions.why: Detail: 'the festival stumbled upon in a small town'.

questions.q: By calling a fully planned journey "a kind of verification", the author implies that such travellers:
opts: Write reviews for other travellers.
Go mainly to confirm what they already expect to see.
Prove that earlier travellers were wrong.
Check the accuracy of their travel documents.
questions.why: Inference: 'we go to confirm that the place matches its picture'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards modern travel conveniences is:
opts: Appreciative, but cautious about relying on them entirely.
Wholly hostile.
Entirely uncritical.
Indifferent.
questions.why: Tone: they 'made travel safer and open to far more people', yet a fully known journey 'risks becoming a kind of verification'.

questions.q: The word "deliberate" in "a deliberate act of openness" most nearly means:
opts: Careless
Slow
Accidental
Intentional
questions.why: Vocabulary: contrasted with 'not out of carelessness'; the blank map is chosen on purpose.

paras: Elections are the most visible moment of a democracy, and the long queues outside polling booths are rightly celebrated. But a citizen who votes once in five years and attends to public affairs at no other time has exercised only a small part of the role. Between elections, the decisions that most affect daily life are taken in municipal councils, village assemblies, school committees and government offices, often in meetings that few citizens attend and through documents that few read. Where the public is absent, those with organised interests, whether contractors, landlords or particular lobbies, are not.

Active citizenship asks more. It includes knowing who one's representatives are and what they have done, attending a ward or gram sabha meeting, using the right to information, and joining with neighbours to raise a common grievance. None of this requires exceptional virtue, but it does require time and a degree of confidence that many people, burdened by work and wary of officialdom, lack. A healthy democracy therefore depends not only on the conscientiousness of individuals but on institutions that make participation practical: meetings held at convenient hours, notices in plain language, and officials who treat questions as a right rather than an annoyance. Democracy, in this sense, is less an event than a habit, and habits must be cultivated.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: Why Officials Dislike Questions
A History of the Gram Sabha
The Mechanics of the Polling Booth
Democracy Between Elections
questions.why: Main idea: citizenship must continue between elections, where most decisions are taken.

questions.q: According to the passage, when the public is absent from local decision-making:
opts: Officials take no decisions at all.
Elections are held earlier than planned.
Those with organised interests, such as contractors and landlords, are still present.
Meetings are cancelled for lack of attendance.
questions.why: Detail: 'Where the public is absent, those with organised interests... are not'.

questions.q: The passage suggests that many people do not participate actively mainly because they:
opts: Are forbidden from attending meetings.
Are uninterested in public affairs.
Believe voting is unimportant.
Lack time and confidence, not because they lack virtue.
questions.why: Inference: participation 'does not require exceptional virtue, but it does require time and a degree of confidence that many people... lack'.

questions.q: The author mentions "meetings held at convenient hours" and "notices in plain language" in order to show that:
opts: Citizens should write the notices themselves.
Officials are mainly to blame for every problem.
Institutions can make participation practical for ordinary people.
Meetings should be held only at night.
questions.why: Purpose: they illustrate 'institutions that make participation practical'.

questions.q: The statement "Democracy... is less an event than a habit" means that democracy:
opts: Happens automatically once a constitution exists.
Depends on continuing participation, not only on periodic voting.
Consists chiefly of election day celebrations.
Is a tradition that cannot be changed.
questions.why: Inference: contrasts the 'event' of elections with ongoing civic practice that 'must be cultivated'.
